outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: The Dispute, the Marks, and the Procedural Path to Appeal
outline.description: This chapter introduces the parties, the competing marks, the services associated with each mark, and the procedural history that brought the case from trademark application and opposition to the Federal Circuit. It frames why the case centers on likelihood of confusion under Section 2(d) of the Lanham Act.
subtopics: CC Serve’s ASPIRE registration: ownership, registration date, and priority date
How CC Serve uses ASPIRE in connection with credit card services through partner banks
Apex Bank’s business model and its planned internet bank under the ASPIRE BANK word and design marks
Apex’s 2019 intent-to-use applications for ASPIRE BANK for 'banking and financing services'
CC Serve’s letter of protest during examination and the marks’ publication despite that protest
The TTAB opposition initiated by CC Serve under Lanham Act Section 2(d)
The Board’s conclusion that confusion was likely and its refusal of registration
Apex’s appeal to the Federal Circuit and the court’s jurisdiction

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: The Governing Framework—Section 2(d), DuPont, and Appellate Review
outline.description: This chapter explains the legal structure the court applies: refusal of registration for likely confusion, the DuPont factor framework, and the division between factual findings and the ultimate legal conclusion. It also clarifies the Federal Circuit’s standards of review and why those standards matter in evaluating the Board’s work.
subtopics: Section 2(d) of the Lanham Act and refusal of registration based on likely confusion
Likelihood of confusion as the ultimate legal question
The DuPont factors as the underlying factual inquiries
The Board’s obligation to consider only the DuPont factors that are relevant and supported by the record
De novo review of legal conclusions by the Federal Circuit
Substantial-evidence review of the Board’s factual findings
Why the distinction between legal error and evidentiary sufficiency is central to this appeal
The specific DuPont factors challenged on appeal: first, second, and sixth

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: The Second DuPont Factor—Similarity of the Parties’ Services
outline.description: This chapter analyzes the court’s treatment of the second DuPont factor, which addresses whether the parties’ services are sufficiently related to support likely confusion. It shows why the Federal Circuit upheld the Board’s analysis on this issue and how that finding became important to the rest of the opinion.
subtopics: The legal standard for relatedness of goods or services: not identity, but relation sufficient to cause consumers to assume a common source
The Board’s effort to define 'credit card services' because the ID Manual entry had been deleted after CC Serve’s registration
The Board’s understanding of 'credit card services' as including issuance, account management, payment processing, monitoring, and related functions
The Board’s reliance on dictionary definitions of 'banking,' 'bank,' and 'finance'
The conclusion that Apex’s 'banking and financing services' and CC Serve’s credit card services are legally identical in part
The Board’s use of third-party registrations to show that these types of services may emanate from a single source under one mark
Apex’s appellate argument that CC Serve is not itself providing banking services but only partnering with banks for card programs
Why the Federal Circuit rejected Apex’s argument and found substantial evidence supporting the Board’s conclusion that the services are highly similar
The significance of affirming this factor: it becomes the baseline for evaluating the Board’s treatment of other factors

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: The Sixth DuPont Factor—Third-Party Use, Mark Strength, and the Error in Defining the Relevant Field
outline.description: This chapter explains the heart of the Federal Circuit’s reversal: the Board’s flawed treatment of third-party use evidence under the sixth DuPont factor. It details how evidence of third-party marks can weaken a mark, how the Board narrowed the relevant universe too much, and why that was inconsistent with its own finding that the parties’ services were highly similar.
subtopics: The sixth DuPont factor: the number and nature of similar marks in use on similar goods or services
Why third-party use matters: it may show that a mark is commercially or conceptually weak and entitled to a narrower scope of protection
The crowded-field rationale: consumers may become accustomed to distinguishing among similar marks
Apex’s evidence of multiple third-party uses and registrations involving 'Aspire' or Aspire-formative marks in financial services
The Board’s decision to limit the relevant public to consumers of credit card services
The Board’s exclusion of marks used for other banking and financing services as 'essentially irrelevant'
The Board’s conclusion that nine credit-card-related uses were insufficient to show weakness
The Board’s resulting determination that ASPIRE was entitled to the normal scope of protection for an inherently distinctive mark
Apex’s argument on appeal that the Board should have considered the broader set of financial-service uses, not only credit-card-specific ones
The Federal Circuit’s legal holding that the sixth factor does not require identical goods or services, only similar ones
The inconsistency identified by the court: the Board found the services highly similar under factor two but applied a narrower similarity standard under factor six
The court’s instruction that the Board should use a consistent scope of similarity across factors once it has found the parties’ services highly similar or partially legally identical
Why the court vacated and remanded rather than deciding the sixth factor itself

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 5: The First DuPont Factor, the Disposition, and the Opinion’s Practical Significance
outline.description: This chapter covers the court’s treatment of the similarity of the marks themselves, the interdependence between mark strength and commercial impression, and the final disposition. It concludes by highlighting the opinion’s significance for TTAB practice and likelihood-of-confusion analysis.
subtopics: The first DuPont factor: similarity of the marks in appearance, sound, connotation, and overall commercial impression
The principle that the marks must be evaluated in their entireties
Why commercial impression can be affected by evidence that a shared term is commercially weak in a crowded field
The Federal Circuit’s decision to vacate the Board’s analysis of the first factor because reconsideration of factor six may alter the strength assessment and thus the marks’ commercial impression
The court’s rejection of the parties’ remaining arguments as unpersuasive
The final judgment: affirming the Board on factor two, vacating on factors six and one, and remanding
Costs awarded to Apex as appellant
The opinion’s doctrinal takeaway: consistency in defining service similarity across DuPont factors
The practical lesson for TTAB litigants: third-party use evidence should be evaluated in light of the full range of similar services recognized elsewhere in the Board’s analysis

The case’s limited but important holding: the Federal Circuit did not decide whether confusion ultimately exists, but required the Board to redo key parts of its analysis under the correct legal approach
